title: The Five Original Translations of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life
excerpt: The Sutra of the Buddha's Infinite Purity and Equal Enlightenment (Han translation)

inline.s: The Sutra of the Buddha's Infinite Purity and Equal Enlightenment (Han translation)
The Sutra of the Buddha's Amita-trayas-triṃśad-buddha-saṃmukha-vasthita-samādhi, Deliverance of Human Beings (Wu translation)
The Sutra of the Buddha's Immeasurable Life (Wei translation)
The Assembly of the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life (Tang translation)
The Sutra of the Buddha's Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life and Adornment (Song translation)
[Amita-trayas-triṃśad-buddha-saṃmukha-vasthita-samādhi, Deliverance of Human Beings] means: the sutra of the Tathāgata Amita's deliverance of human beings.
[Amita]
Amita
, in Chinese translation: immeasurable.

[Amita-trayas-triṃśad-buddha-saṃmukha-vasthita-samādhi] is an honorific title of the Tathāgata. [Deliverance] means to carry beings across, to bring them out of birth and death. The Sutra of the Buddha's Infinite Purity and Equal Enlightenment (Han translation) says:
“When I become Buddha, may I be as the Dharma King: delivering all from birth and death, leaving none unreleased.”
[Human realm] is one of the six realms (devas, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hells); that is, what is commonly called “the human world.”

inline.s: Translated by the Tripiṭaka master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi country in the Later Han

blocks.text: The Sutra of the Buddha's Infinite Purity and Equal Enlightenment, Scroll One

inline.s: The Buddha was in the Vulture Peak in the country of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of disciples: twelve hundred and fifty persons, seventy-two nayutas of bodhisattvas, five hundred nuns, seven thousand laymen, five hundred laywomen, eight hundred thousand desire-realm devas, seven hundred thousand form-realm devas, sixty nayutas of devas of Pervasive Purity, and a hundred million Brahmā gods — all dwelling with the Buddha.
[Nayuta] is also written nayuta; it corresponds to a koṭi in our lands.

The disciples of supernormal powers and miraculous flight were named: the worthy Knower of the Ultimate Bound, the worthy Horse-Trainer, the worthy Great Strength, the worthy Serene, the worthy Able in Praise, the worthy Arm of Fulfilled Vows, the worthy Dust-Free, the worthy Kāśyapa of the Clan Assembled, the worthy Bull-Cud (chī), the worthy Timely Kāśyapa, the worthy Constant Kāśyapa, the worthy Golden Pestle Kāśyapa, the worthy Śāriputra, the worthy Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the worthy Mahākāśyapa, the worthy Mahākātyāyana (zhān), the worthy Great Sleeper, the worthy Great Merchant, the worthy Tall and Lean, the worthy Full of Discernment, the worthy Strife-Free, the worthy Knower of Past Lives, the worthy Comprehender of Profound Samādhi, the worthy Welcome One, the worthy Revatī, the worthy King of Fools, the worthy Clan of Pure Precepts, the worthy Kin-Loving, the worthy Scriptural Brahmin, the worthy Full of Desire, the worthy Palace-Born, the worthy Summoned, the worthy Black Mountain, the worthy Royal Kṣatriya, the worthy Wide-Learned.

His female disciples were named: the nun Great Reverence, the nun Illusionist, the nun Lotus-Hued, the nun Earth-Shaking, the nun Earth-Bearing, the nun At Whose Birth Her Attendant's Head Ached, the nun Peaceful Increase, the nun Soft of Body, the nun Courageous in Practice, and the nun Self-Purified.

The laymen were named: the elder Giver to the Destitute and Solitary, the elder Mindful of the Assembly, the elder Swift of Arm, the elder Fire Blossom, the elder Good Countenance, the elder Perfect Treasure, the elder Widely Renowned, the elder Fragrance Averting Plague, the elder Peace and Auspice, the elder Treasure of Abundant Giving, the elder Joyful Praise, the elder Earnest in Fetal Offering, the elder Serving Other Paths, the elder Courage Vanquishing Enmity, the elder Jeweled Earring, and the elder Jeweled Knot.

The laywomen were named: one called Lesser Sheath (lǚ), one called Black Wisdom, one called Faith in Dharma, one called Gentle Goodness, one called Joyful Coolness, one called Bearing Suffering with Joy, and one called Joyful Love, an upāsikā.
Beings such as these were all of one kind: those who have dissolved every defilement, the pure and valiant. Countless multitudes were all gathered together in one great assembly.

At that time the Buddha sat contemplating the true path, and on his face there was light of nine colors, shifting through many thousands of hues, its radiance exceedingly bright. The worthy Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, knelt with palms joined, and said to the Buddha: “Now the light and color of the Buddha's face — why does it change from moment to moment, and shine thus? Now the Buddha's countenance is luminous, of many hundreds of thousands of colors, radiant above and below, fair beyond words. Since I began attending the Buddha I have never seen the Buddha's body so shining, so towering in its doubled brightness. Never have I seen the Perfectly Enlightened One's radiance and majesty as it is today, so fair and true. Can it be that you are recollecting the Buddhas of the past and the future, or the Buddhas now present in other regions?”
The Buddha told Ānanda: “Was it some deva who came to instruct you, or the Buddhas who instructed you, that made you question me? Or did it come of your own wisdom?”

Ānanda said to the Buddha: “It was no deva, and no instruction of the Buddhas. That I now question the Buddha came of my own mind; I have come to tell the Buddha of it. Whenever the Buddha sits or rises, walks, comes in or goes out, arrives somewhere, does what is to be done, or gives what is to be taught, I at once know the Buddha's mind. Now the Buddha is alone, turning something over and over in his thought, and so the light of his countenance is like this.”

The Buddha said: “Excellent, Ānanda. What you have asked is profoundly deep and wholly good; it will bring deliverance to many. To question the Buddha surpasses offering to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of a whole world. To give in charity to the devas and people, and to the winged and crawling creatures, for kalpas on end, exceeds it by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of times.”
The Buddha said: “Ānanda, the devas, kings, and people of this time, and the winged and crawling creatures as well — you shall deliver them all.”

The Buddha said: “The Buddha's majestic power is very weighty and hard to withstand, and what you have asked is greatly profound. You have a heart of compassion, and you grieve for the Buddha's sake. The devas and people, and monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, are greatly good. In every case, deliver them all.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “In the world there is the udumbara tree: it bears fruit, but has no flower. Only when a Buddha appears in the world does its flower come forth. A Buddha's appearing in the world is very hard to meet. Now I have become Buddha and appeared in the world. If there is one of great virtue, wise and good of heart, who foresees the Buddha's mind, he will not forget to be at the Buddha's side attending him. As for what you now ask, listen well! Listen with attention!”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “In the kalpas already past, the multitudes were countless and immeasurable, boundless and beyond reckoning. At that time there was a past Buddha named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata; then again there was a Buddha named Blazing Light; then again a Buddha named Sun-Moon Fragrance; then again a Buddha named Mount Peaceful Brightness; then again a Buddha named Sun-Moon Countenance; then again a Buddha named Dust-Free; then again a Buddha named Unstained; then again a Buddha named Like a Dragon That Subdues All; then again a Buddha named Sunlight; then again a Buddha named King of Great Sound; then again a Buddha named Jewel Purity and Brightness; then again a Buddha named Golden Treasury; then again a Buddha named Flame-Jewel Light; then again a Buddha named Uplifted Earth; then again a Buddha named Vaiḍūrya Light; then again a Buddha named Sun-Moon Light; then again a Buddha named Sun Voice; then again a Buddha named Light Blossom; then again a Buddha named Supernormal Power Roaming, Holding the Mind Like the Sea; then again a Buddha named Exalted Praise; then again a Buddha named Perfect Jewel Purity; then again a Buddha named Light That Opens and Transforms; then again a Buddha named Great Fragrance Renowned; then again a Buddha named Conquering and Casting Off Wrath and Envy; then again a Buddha named Wondrous Vaiḍūrya Purple-Ground Gold Flame; then again a Buddha named Mind-Holding Dharma Blossom, None Surpassing; then again a Buddha named Heap of Many Blossoms; then again a Buddha named Water-Moon Light; then again a Buddha named Dispelling All Darkness; then again a Buddha named Sunlight Canopy; then again a Buddha named Tathāgata Mild and Harmonious; then again a Buddha named Dharma Mind; then again a Buddha named Lion's Majesty, Elephant-King's Stride; then again a Buddha named World's Hero; then again a Buddha named Pure Sound; then again a Buddha named Unconquerable.

Then again there was a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja. He taught there for forty-two kalpas; all these have already passed, and it was in that kalpa that he became Buddha. Among devas above and humans below, the hero of human beings; in the teachings of the path and Dharma, a valiant general. When the Buddha taught the sutras and expounded the path for the devas and the people of the world, none could surpass him.

King Lokeśvararāja heard the sutra teaching, rejoiced, and understood. He then abandoned his throne, went forth as a monk, and was named Dharmākara. He brought forth the bodhisattva resolve and was a man of lofty talent. In wisdom and courage none could surpass him, and he was wholly unlike the world. He came to where the Buddha Lokeśvararāja was, bowed his head in homage, knelt with palms joined, and praised the Buddha in these words:
The light beyond all measure, majesty without any end.
Such is this blazing radiance, none can be its equal.
Though sun and maṇi, fire, moon and water take their forms,
their light cannot come near it, their colors cannot compare.
Its countenance none can measure, foremost in all the world.
So great is this sound of his, it reaches countless lands.
By samādhi and absorption, by effort and by wisdom,
majesty and virtue unmatched, surpassing and most rare.
In profound and subtle truth, in good and mindful thought,
the Buddha's Dharma is attained; hence it comes to be.
The awakened held like an ocean, whose bounds have no bottom.
Anger and ignorance: these the World-Honored One does not have.
Praising the Buddha, the world's hero, from first to last, never weary.
The Buddha is like a fair flowering tree; there is none who does not love it.
People in every place who see him all rejoice.
When I become Buddha, may I be as the Dharma King.
Delivering all from birth and death, leaving none unreleased.
Giving and taming the mind, precepts, patience, and effort.
Such samādhi and absorption, wisdom is the highest and the best.
If I vow to attain Buddhahood, may I fully reach all these things.
For all fears and terrors, I shall win great peace.
Though there were a hundred thousand, a billion nayutas of Buddhas,
though the number of such Buddhas were as the sands of the Ganges,
and one made offering to all those Buddhas, count for count,
it would not equal seeking the true path, firm and brave and undismayed.
Suppose in the Ganges' waters, world systems of flowing sand,
and again beyond all reckoning, lands without number:
the light of his flame illumines all, throughout those countless lands.
Such is the power of his effort, his majesty beyond all measure.
May I be made the world's hero, my land the foremost of all.
Its assembly excellent and fair, its bodhi site beyond all lands.
A land like to nirvāṇa's realm, and without equal or twin.
I shall ever be compassionate, delivering every being.
Those born there from the ten directions, their hearts rejoice and are pure.
Having come to my land, in joy and peace they dwell.
May the Buddha but believe and know me: this is my first witness.
I myself vow to be in that land; effort's power is what I seek.
The World-Honored Ones of the ten directions all have unobstructed wisdom;
they ever call to mind this hero, and they know the mind I tread.
Though my body abide in every place of bitter poison,
I shall practice the power of effort and endure, never repenting.

When the bhikṣu Dharma-Treasury had spoken this praise of the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, perfectly enlightened, he brought forth the intention to seek supreme, true, and perfect enlightenment: “I establish this vow: whatever the Tathāgata has attained, may I obtain it all. Pulling beings up from toil and suffering, from the root of birth and death, may I make them all as the Buddha. Only do you expound the sutra and the practices to be carried out, that I may swiftly reach resolve. When I become Buddha, let nothing come near me. May the Buddha tell me of the merits of the Buddhas' lands: I shall receive and uphold them, and shall dwell therein. I take this vow to become Buddha, and my land shall be likewise.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The Buddha Lokeśvararāja knew that he was lofty and wise and that his vow was wholly good, and at once expounded the sutra for the Bodhisattva Dharma-Treasury, saying: Suppose the waters of the great sea — one man draws them up measure by measure, and for a whole kalpa does not stop: the sea may yet run dry and be emptied to the mud at its bottom. If a man seeks the path with a whole heart, how should it be that he cannot attain it? Let him seek and strive without resting; he will surely gain what his heart desires.

When the Bodhisattva Dharma-Treasury heard the Buddha Lokeśvararāja expound the sutra in this way, he was filled with great joy and leaped up. That Buddha then chose for him, out of two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands, the good and the ugly of their devas and people, and of their lands, good and evil. He chose according to what his heart desired and gave it to him. When the Buddha Lokeśvararāja had finished expounding the sutra, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Treasury made his mind one, and at once obtained the divine eye of perfect sight, seeing of himself, in all those two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands, the good and evil of the devas and people and the good and ugly of the lands. He then chose according to what his heart desired, and so formed these twenty-four vows, receiving and upholding that sutra.

Strenuous and courageous, he toiled and sought. For kalpas without bound he served and made offering to the Buddhas; the Buddhas of the past were likewise without bound. In the end, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Treasury himself attained Buddhahood, with the name Immeasurable Purity and Enlightenment, Most Venerable. His wisdom was courageous, his radiance without equal. He is now present, and the land in which he dwells is wholly good and fair. In another region, a Buddha-land apart, he teaches the devas and people, above and below, throughout the eight directions, without bound, and the winged and crawling creatures as well: none who does not attain deliverance from grief and suffering. When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows, treasured and prized them, upheld them with reverence, and strove in Chan practice; he was set apart from the assembly, pre-eminent and wholly different, and none could equal him.”
The Buddha said: “What are these twenty-four vows?

1. When I become Buddha, let there be in my land no hells, no birds and beasts, no hungry ghosts, no winged or crawling creatures. Only when I obtain this vow shall I become Buddha; if I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become Buddha.

2. When I become Buddha, let the people in my land — those who come to be born in my land, and those who depart from my land — never again pass into hells, hungry ghosts, birds and beasts, or crawling things. If any be born among them, I shall not become Buddha.
3. When I become Buddha, if the people who come to be born in my land are not of one color and kind, golden-hued, I shall not become Buddha.
4. When I become Buddha, if among the people who come to be born in my land there be any difference between devas and humans in the world, I shall not become Buddha.

5. When I become Buddha, let the people who come to be born in my land all know of themselves the beginning and end of the lives from which they came, and the past lives of a billion kalpas from which they came. If they do not all know and recall the lives from which they came, I shall not become Buddha.
6. When I become Buddha, if the people who come to be born in my land do not all have perfect sight, I shall not become Buddha.
7. When I become Buddha, if the people who come to be born in my land do not all know the thoughts in the minds of others, I shall not become Buddha.
8. When I become Buddha, if the people in my land do not all fly, I shall not become Buddha.
9. When I become Buddha, if the people in my land do not all hear perfectly, I shall not become Buddha.
10. When I become Buddha, if the people in my land have any craving or desire, I shall not become Buddha.
11. When I become Buddha, let the people in my land abide and at the last enter parinirvāṇa. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.

12. When I become Buddha, let the disciples in my land — throughout the eight directions, above and below, in each of a thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands, let the devas and people and crawling creatures become great disciples of pratyekabuddha rank, all with minds unified in Chan, and together count the disciples in my land: though they abide at it for a hundred koṭis of kalpas, let none be able to count them. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.

13. When I become Buddha, let my radiance surpass the sun and moon; let the light of the Buddhas be hundreds of billions of times greater, illumining countless worlds; and wherever there is darkness, let it be ever wholly bright. Let the devas and people and crawling creatures, seeing my light, all turn to kind hearts and good deeds and come to be born in my land. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.

14. When I become Buddha, let the devas and people and crawling creatures of the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above and below — let them attain the fruit and realization of pratyekabuddha disciples, sit in Chan with minds unified, and wish together to know how many thousands of koṭis of kalpas my life shall last: let none be able to know the limit or bottom of my lifespan. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.

15. When I become Buddha, as for the people who come to be born in my land, apart from the vows of the people in my own land, the lifespan of the rest of the people shall be beyond all reckoning. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.
16. When I become Buddha, let all the people in my land be without an evil thought. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.

17. When I become Buddha, let my fame be heard throughout the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below; let the Buddhas each among their assemblies of disciples praise the goodness of my merit and my land; and let the devas and people and crawling creatures, hearing my name, all leap up and come to be born in my land. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.

18. When I become Buddha, as for the people of the Buddha-lands who walk the bodhisattva path and ever call to mind the purity of my heart: at the end of their lives I, with countless bhikṣus, shall fly to welcome them and stand before them, and they shall at once be born again in my land, attaining the stage of non-retrogression. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.

19. When I become Buddha, as for the people of Buddha-lands in other regions who did evil in former lives, if they hear my name and set their minds rightly on the path, wishing to come to be born in my land: at the end of their lives let them never again pass through the three evil paths, but be born in my land according to what their hearts desire. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.
20. When I become Buddha, let the bodhisattvas in my land not attain the single birth and set aside these other vows and merits. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.
21. When I become Buddha, if the bodhisattvas in my land do not all possess the thirty-two marks, I shall not become Buddha.

22. When I become Buddha, when the bodhisattvas in my land wish to make offering together to the countless Buddhas throughout the eight directions, above and below, let them all fly; and when they wish for ten thousand kinds of things produced of themselves, let these appear before them, and let them take them to make offering to the Buddhas. And when the offering is complete, before the sun has passed its height, let them return to my land. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.

23. When I become Buddha, when the bodhisattvas in my land wish to eat, let food of a hundred flavors arise of itself in bowls of seven treasures and appear before them. When they have eaten, let the bowls vanish of themselves. If it be not so, I shall not become Buddha.
24. When I become Buddha, if the bodhisattvas in my land, in expounding the sutras and walking the path, be not as the Buddha, I shall not become Buddha.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows. He gave in charity and shared out his goods, and never transgressed the precepts of the path. He was patient and strenuous, single-minded in wisdom. His vow and aspiration were ever courageous; he never slandered the sutra teachings and never slackened in his seeking. Again and again he abandoned his kingdom and gave up his throne, cut himself off from wealth and desire, and with clear discernment sought his vow, turning toward nothing else. He piled up merit and gathered virtue for kalpas without bound, and of himself attained Buddhahood, fully obtaining them all. He did not forget his merit.”

The Buddha said: “The radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most honored, the first, without equal; the radiance of all the Buddhas cannot come near it. Among the countless Buddhas throughout the eight directions, above and below, there is a Buddha whose crown light shines seven zhang; there is one whose crown light shines one li; there is one whose crown light shines five li; there is one whose crown light shines twenty li; there is one whose crown light shines forty li; there is one whose crown light shines eighty li; there is one whose crown light shines a hundred and sixty li; there is one whose crown light shines three hundred and twenty li; there is one whose crown light shines six hundred and forty li; there is one whose crown light shines one thousand three hundred li; there is one whose crown light shines two thousand six hundred li; there is one whose crown light shines five thousand two hundred li; there is one whose crown light shines ten thousand four hundred li; there is one whose crown light shines twenty-one thousand li; there is one whose crown light shines forty-two thousand li; there is one whose crown light shines eighty-four thousand li; there is one whose crown light shines a hundred and seventy thousand li; there is one whose crown light shines three hundred and fifty thousand li; there is one whose crown light shines seven hundred thousand li; there is one whose crown light shines one million five hundred thousand li; there is one whose crown light shines three million li; there is one whose crown light shines six million li; there is one whose crown light shines twelve million li; there is one whose crown light shines one Buddha-land; there is one whose crown light shines two Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines four Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines eight Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines fifteen Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines thirty Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines sixty Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines a hundred and twenty Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines five hundred Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines a thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines two thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines four thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines eight thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines sixteen thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines thirty-two thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines sixty-four thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines a hundred and thirty thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines two hundred and sixty thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines five hundred thousand Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines a million Buddha-lands; there is one whose crown light shines two million Buddha-lands.”

The Buddha said: “The crown light of the countless Buddhas throughout the eight directions, above and below, shines in just these ways. The crown light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity blazes across a thousand myriad Buddha-lands. Why is it that the light of the Buddhas shines near or far? In former lives, when they sought the path as bodhisattvas, the merit of their vows was each greater or lesser, and when at last they became Buddhas they each obtained accordingly. Therefore their light is not equal; yet the majestic power of the Buddhas is equal. They act freely as their minds desire, without forethought. The light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity shines the farthest; the light of all the Buddhas cannot come near it.”

The Buddha praised the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity: “The radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is exceedingly good, good and bright and fair, most joyful and without equal, utterly peerless beyond measure.

The radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is so excellent that it surpasses the light of sun and moon by hundreds of billions of times; the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the brightest of all the Buddhas' radiance; the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the fairest of all the Buddhas' radiance; the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most heroic of all the Buddhas' radiance; the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most joyful and good of all the Buddhas' radiance; the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the king of all the Buddhas' radiance; the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most honored of all the Buddhas' radiance; the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the light of life among all the Buddhas' radiance, without limit; and its flame illumines the countless dark places of the worlds, so that all are ever bright.

All the people, the winged creatures, and the crawling things — there are none who do not see the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity. Seeing the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, there are none who do not turn to kind hearts and rejoice. All the world's lust, anger, and ignorance — seeing the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, there are none who do not do good. In the hells, among the beasts, and among the hungry ghosts, in every place of torment and bitter toil, when the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity arrives, all cease and are tormented no more, and after death none fail to be released from grief and suffering.

The radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is famed throughout the eight directions, above and below, endless and boundless, in countless Buddha-lands. There are no devas or people who do not hear of it. And of those who hear of it, there are none who do not attain deliverance.”

The Buddha said: “It is not I alone who praise the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity. The countless Buddhas throughout the eight directions, above and below, together with the pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats, all praise it in just this way.”

The Buddha said: “Should there be people, good men and good women, who hear the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and praise his radiance — thus morning and evening ever praising the brightness and fairness of that light, with a whole heart and without ceasing — then according to what their hearts desire, wishing to be born in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, they may be revered by all the bodhisattvas and arhats, and be wise and courageous. And if afterward they become Buddhas, they shall likewise be praised for their radiance by the countless pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats throughout the eight directions, above and below, in just this way; and the assembled bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, and arhats, and the devas, kings, and people, hearing of it, shall all rejoice and leap up, and there shall be none who do not praise them.”

The Buddha said: “Were I to speak of the beauty of the radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and praise its majesty and excellent goodness, a whole kalpa of days and nights would not yet exhaust it; I have told you only a little of it.”

When the Buddha had spoken of the quest of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and of his obtaining these twenty-four vows, Prince Ajātaśatru and the sons of five hundred great elders, each holding a golden flower canopy, came before the Buddha and offered them; then they all withdrew and sat to one side to hear the sutra. When Prince Ajātaśatru and the sons of the five hundred elders heard the twenty-four vows of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, they were filled with great joy and leaped up. In their hearts they all made this vow: when we afterward become Buddhas, may we all be as the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity. The Buddha knew this, and told the assembled bhikṣus: “This Prince Ajātaśatru and the sons of the five hundred elders shall, after countless kalpas, all become Buddhas, as the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity.”

The Buddha said: “This Prince Ajātaśatru and the sons of the five hundred elders, since they began walking the bodhisattva path, for countless kalpas have each made offering to four hundred koṭis of Buddhas, and now again they come to make offering to me. This Prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred others were all disciples of mine in former lives, in the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa. Now they are all gathered again; this is their meeting once more.” Then the assembled bhikṣus, hearing the Buddha's words, were all elated in heart, and there were none who did not rejoice.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Since the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity became Buddha, eighteen kalpas have passed. The land in which he dwells is named Sukhāvatī, and it lies directly to the west, a thousand koṭis of Mount Sumeru Buddha-lands away from this land of Jambudvīpa. The ground of that land is all naturally of the seven treasures. The first treasure is called silver. The second treasure is called gold. The third treasure is crystal. The fourth treasure is lapis lazuli. The fifth treasure is coral. The sixth treasure is amber. The seventh treasure is tridacna shell. These seven treasures all serve one another as ground, vast and exceedingly great beyond measure, each mingling with the others and passing into one another. Each blazes with its own light, and their mingled light is exceedingly bright. Naturally soft and exceedingly fair beyond compare. Like that ground of seven treasures. All the finest of the many treasures throughout the eight directions, above and below, come together naturally and are born by transformation in common; and these treasures are like the seven treasures of the sixth heaven above.

In that land there is no Mount Sumeru; its sun, moon, and stars, the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, and the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa all dwell in the open sky. In that land there is no great ocean, nor any small sea, nor rivers or streams, nor mountains and forests, valleys and ravines, nor any place of darkness.

The seven-treasure ground of that land is everywhere level and even. There are no hells, no birds and beasts, no hungry ghosts, no winged or crawling creatures, no asuras, no dragons, spirits, or ghosts. There is never any time of great rain, nor any spring, summer, autumn, or winter. There is no great cold, nor any great heat. It is ever temperate and moderate, most joyful and good beyond compare, and all things of ten thousand kinds arise naturally. Of foods of a hundred flavors, whatever the mind wishes to obtain appears of itself before one. And what the mind does not want vanishes of itself. Like the natural things of the sixth heaven above, freely as one wishes, all according to one's mind.

In that land all are bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and their lifespan is exceedingly long, beyond countless kalpas. Women who are born there are born by transformation, all becoming male. There are only bodhisattvas and arhats beyond number, all with perfect sight and perfect hearing, all seeing one another from afar, gazing at one another from afar, hearing one another's voices from afar; all are seekers of the path and doers of good, of one single kind, with no different sorts among them. Those bodhisattvas and arhats all have upright and proper features, pure and exceedingly fair, all of one color, with none who is one-sided or ugly.

The bodhisattvas and arhats are all talented, bold, and wise. As for their clothing, they all wear clothing that arises naturally; whatever their hearts hold, they ever keep virtue in mind; and whatever they wish to say, they all know one another's meaning beforehand. What they keep in mind is the path. They ever speak of the five matters. The bodhisattvas and arhats in that land, when they speak with one another, at once speak of the sutras and the path, and never speak of the faults of others. The sound of their speech is like three hundred bells. They all revere and love one another, and none hate another; all speak according to elder and younger, high and low, in order, and they all gather together and meet with righteousness and courtesy. They revere and serve one another as elder brother and younger brother. They walk in benevolence and tread in righteousness; they act without rashness, and their words are truthful; they teach and command one another and do not go against one another; they receive and uphold from one another, and all are pure of heart, without greed or envy. Never is there any lust, any heart of anger, any manner of ignorance. There is no crooked mind, no thought turned toward women. All are wise and courageous, harmonious in mind and joyful. They love the sutras and the path, and all know of themselves the lives from which they came in former ages — the good and evil, the living and dying, of billions of kalpas of past lives — and what is present they know without limit.

The places where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity may teach — the lecture halls and monasteries — are all likewise of the natural seven treasures. Gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and tridacna shell all transform and complete one another. They are exceedingly beautiful and bright, utterly fair beyond compare. There is no maker of them, nor is it known whence they come, nor is there anyone who brings them, nor anywhere they go. Because the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity's vow and virtue are weighty, and because those people do good, they discuss the meaning of the sutras, expound the sutras and walk the path, and hold their assemblies within them — and these arise by natural transformation. Those lecture halls and monasteries all have towers, galleries, railings, and balustrades of the seven treasures. They are further adorned with gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and tridacna shell; and further interwoven with white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and maṇi pearls, spread over them; and all of themselves give forth the five tones, their sound exceedingly fair beyond compare.

In the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, the dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats are all likewise of the seven treasures — gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, tridacna shell, and agate — born by transformation and completing one another. Their dwellings all have towers, galleries, railings, and balustrades of the seven treasures. They are further adorned with gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and tridacna shell. And further interwoven with white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and maṇi pearls, spread over them; and each of them likewise gives forth the five tones of itself. In the lecture halls and monasteries of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and in the seven-treasure dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats, within and without, in every place, there are further naturally flowing springs and bathing pools. Those bathing pools are all again of the natural seven treasures. The seven treasures are all born together: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and tridacna shell, transforming and completing one another. The sand at the bottom of the water is all again of the seven treasures: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and tridacna shell. There are pools of pure silver, whose bottom sand is all gold. There are pools of pure gold, whose bottom sand is all silver. There are pools of pure crystal, whose bottom sand is all lapis lazuli. There are pools of pure lapis lazuli, whose bottom sand is all crystal. There are pools of pure coral, whose bottom sand is all amber. There are pools of pure amber, whose bottom sand is all coral. There are pools of pure tridacna shell, whose bottom sand is all agate. There are pools of pure agate, whose bottom sand is all tridacna shell. There are pools of pure white jade, whose bottom sand is all purple-ground gold. There are pools of pure purple-ground gold, whose bottom sand is all white jade. There are again pools made of two treasures together, whose bottom sand is all gold and silver. There are again pools made of three treasures together, whose bottom sand is all gold, silver, and crystal. There are again pools made of four treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. There are again pools made of five treasures together, whose bottom sand is all gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, and amber. There are again pools made of six treasures together, whose bottom sand is all gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and tridacna shell. There are again pools made of seven treasures together, whose bottom sand is all gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, tridacna shell, and agate.

Among those bathing pools there are some forty li long. There are pools eighty li long. There are pools a hundred and sixty li long. There are pools three hundred and twenty li long. There are pools six hundred and forty li long. There are pools one thousand two hundred and eighty li long. There are bathing pools two thousand five hundred and sixty li long. There are bathing pools five thousand one hundred and twenty li long. There are bathing pools ten thousand two hundred and forty li long. There are bathing pools twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li long. Their length and breadth are each exactly equal. These bathing pools are the pools in which all the bodhisattvas and arhats ever bathe.”

The Buddha said: “The bathing pool of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is forty-eight thousand li long, and forty-eight thousand li broad. Its bathing pool is all made by the seven treasures transforming and completing one another. The sand at the bottom of its water is all again of the seven treasures, white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and maṇi pearls. The water in the bathing pool of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and of the bodhisattvas and arhats, is all pure, fragrant, and clean. In it there are fragrant flowers, a hundred kinds of flowers all born naturally, of many kinds and different colors and different fragrances, the flowers all with a thousand petals; the flowers are exceedingly fragrant beyond compare, their fragrance beyond words. The fragrance of those flowers is again not that of worldly flowers; it surpasses even the flowers of heaven. The fragrance of those flowers is the finest among all the flower fragrances of the eight directions, above and below, born naturally. The water in the pool flows and pours into itself, one into another. The water flowing in the pool is neither slow nor swift, and all of itself gives forth the five tones.”

The Buddha said: “The devas and people, and the winged and crawling creatures, of the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above and below — all who are born in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity are born by transformation in the lotus flowers of that seven-treasure water. They at once grow naturally, and there is none who nurses them; they all eat natural food and drink. As for their bodies, they are neither the bodies of worldly people nor the bodies of heavenly people: they are all compounded of the virtue of many good deeds, and all receive bodies of natural emptiness, exceedingly fair beyond compare.”

The Buddha said: “Ānanda, suppose a poor beggar in the world were made to dwell beside a king: what would the man's face and features be like? Would they be like the king's face, features, and complexion?”

Ānanda said: “Even if one made such a man dwell beside a king, his face and features would be exceedingly ugly and uncomely; they would not be like the king's face, whose features are fair, by a hundred thousand billion times. Why is this? Because one sees that the beggar is poor and utterly destitute, and has never had a time of fine food. Since his food is coarse, he cannot get enough to eat. He eats only to keep his life going, his joints propping one another up, with nothing to supply himself. He is ever lacking and has no store: hungry, cold, and frozen, frightened and grieving. All this because in former lives, when he was a person, he was foolish and without wisdom, and the richer he grew the stingier he became. Having wealth, he would not show compassion or kindness, would not give to the worthy and good, would not do good or love widely or give in charity, but only wished to get things for nothing, grudging food and drink, eating delicacies alone, not believing that what is given or lent will be repaid hereafter. And he did not believe that doing good brings blessing in later lives. Muddy and stubborn, he did more and more evil. Thus at the end of his life his goods were utterly exhausted. Having never any kindness or virtue, he had nothing to rely on. He entered the evil paths, and suffered there accordingly. Only after that did he get out and find release, and now in this life he is born a person, born as a child into a low and poor family. Barely in human shape, his appearance is exceedingly ugly; his clothing is worn and torn, and he stands alone and empty, unable to cover his body, living as a beggar. Hungry and cold, afflicted by suffering, his face is gaunt and mean, and he does not look of human color. All this because of what his own body did in former lives: he receives its penalty, shown to the multitude, and there is none to pity him. Cast out on the highways and markets, exposed and wasted away, black and ugly and utterly vile, he is not the equal of a human being.
